topics.title: Borrowing is not ownership
topics.summary: A reference lets one part of a program use an existing object. It does not keep that object alive. A design must state which object is responsible for destruction and which users must finish first.

concepts.definition: Use an existing object without taking responsibility for destroying it. The owner must outlive the use.

cards.question: Does holding a reference extend an ordinary existing object’s lifetime?
cards.answer: No. If its owner destroys it, a stored reference becomes dangling. Arrange the lifetimes or select an appropriate ownership model.

scenario.prompt: A report stores const Writer&. The function creating its local Writer returns before the report is used. What must the design address?
options: The report may outlive its borrowed Writer.
A reference always copies its object.
Making render virtual extends every argument’s lifetime.
scenario.explanation: The reference borrows the local Writer, whose lifetime ends when the function returns. Keep the Writer alive for every use or let the report own an appropriate object.
rationales: Correct: the borrower needs a live object during every access.
const restricts modification through that access path; it does not extend lifetime.
A reference aliases an existing object rather than copying it.
Virtual dispatch chooses an overriding function; it does not keep unrelated objects alive.
